# Draft:Wifi Aware

----
Wi-Fi Aware is a proximity-based wireless discovery and peer-to-peer communication technology standardized by the Wi-Fi Alliance. It is based on IEEE 802.11 amendments originally known as the Neighbor Awareness Networking (NAN) specification. Wi-Fi Aware enables devices to discover each other and exchange data without requiring an Internet connection or a traditional Wi-Fi access point, instead forming direct links over Wi-Fi.
Wi-Fi Aware is designed for applications such as local file sharing, multiplayer gaming, social discovery, device provisioning, and Internet of Things (IoT) interactions. The technology is defined by the Wi-Fi Alliance as one of several "alternative topologies", alongside Wi-Fi Direct and Tunneled Direct Link Setup (TDLS).
Overview
Wi-Fi Aware allows nearby devices to publish and subscribe to services using a continuous scan and synchronization mechanism. When matching services are detected, devices may establish a higher-bandwidth data path using either Wi-Fi NAN Data Paths (NDPs) or conventional Wi-Fi Direct links.
Unlike traditional Wi-Fi scanning, Wi-Fi Aware maintains a synchronized discovery window schedule between participating devices to reduce power consumption and maintain consistent discovery performance.
History
Wi-Fi Aware grew out of work in the IEEE 802.11 working groups to standardize proximity-based service discovery and neighbor awareness. In the mid-2010s the Wi-Fi Alliance introduced NAN-based peer-to-peer discovery under the marketing name Wi-Fi Aware, positioning it as an alternative topology alongside Wi-Fi Direct and TDLS.
Early chipset support appeared in platforms from Broadcom, Qualcomm and other vendors beginning in 2016–2017, enabling always-on discovery and NAN data paths in smartphones and IoT devices.
Android added native platform support for Wi-Fi Aware in Android 8.0 (2017). Many Android devices shipped since 2018 include compatible hardware.
In 2025, analysis of European Union Digital Markets Act (DMA) interoperability requirements indicated that Apple would be required to support Wi-Fi Aware in future iOS releases, and to deprecate its proprietary Apple Wireless Direct Link (AWDL) protocol for peer-to-peer Wi-Fi in the EU.
Technical operation
Wi-Fi Aware defines two major components: a discovery mechanism and a data transport mechanism.
Discovery engine (NAN discovery)
Devices participate in synchronized discovery windows to transmit:
* service hash IDs
* publish/subscribe frames
* device capabilities
* master synchronization beacons
Devices elect a master node to coordinate the timing of availability windows, in order to align wake-up times and limit energy consumption.
Data transport (NAN Data Paths)
Once two devices match a service, they may establish:
* NDPs — direct, encrypted Wi-Fi NAN data paths
* Wi-Fi Direct — as a fallback for devices lacking full NAN data support
Transport uses standard 802.11 PHY and MAC framing over dynamically selected channels.
IPv6 addressing
After establishing an NDP, devices typically exchange link-local IPv6 addresses for direct communication, without requiring DHCP or a router.
Implementations
Android
Android 8.0 and later include support for Wi-Fi Aware discovery and data paths through the WifiAwareManager API. Android documentation notes that Wi-Fi Aware can be used by applications to create and manage publish/subscribe sessions and to establish NAN data paths for higher-bandwidth transport.
Android networking documentation also describes how Wi-Fi Aware and other Wi-Fi scanning mechanisms coexist with infrastructure Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi Direct in order to provide proximity-based services.
Apple platforms
Apple provides a WiFiAware framework in its developer documentation for managing Wi-Fi Aware sessions and peer discovery on supported platforms.
In the context of EU DMA interoperability enforcement, industry commentators report that Apple is expected to transition AirDrop and related features from AWDL to standards-based Wi-Fi Aware in future iOS and macOS releases, enabling cross-platform peer-to-peer Wi-Fi with other vendors’ devices.
Chipsets
Commercial Wi-Fi Aware support is available in several Wi-Fi system-on-chip (SoC) families, including:
* Qualcomm Atheros and FastConnect platforms
* Broadcom Wi-Fi 5, Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 6E chipsets
* Select MediaTek Wi-Fi 5/6 SoCs
Support is typically exposed through platform-specific drivers and operating-system APIs rather than directly to end users.
Relationship to other technologies
Comparison with Wi-Fi Direct
Wi-Fi Direct creates a temporary network with a group owner (similar to an access point). Wi-Fi Aware, by contrast:
* performs continuous discovery of nearby devices
* does not require forming a full Wi-Fi infrastructure network
* allows multicast-style service announcements
* uses synchronized availability windows to save power
Wi-Fi Direct is commonly used for bulk transport (for example, file transfers and media streaming), whereas Wi-Fi Aware is optimized for real-time proximity recognition and service discovery, and can then be combined with Wi-Fi Direct or NAN data paths for data transfer.
Comparison with Apple's AWDL
Apple Wireless Direct Link (AWDL), used internally by Apple for AirDrop, Handoff and other services, implements similar concepts—synchronized availability windows and direct IPv6 communication—but is proprietary and not interoperable with Wi-Fi Aware.
Under pressure from EU DMA interoperability requirements, Apple is expected to phase out AWDL in favor of Wi-Fi Aware on its platforms, which would allow standards-based cross-platform peer-to-peer Wi-Fi between Apple and non-Apple devices.
Applications
Wi-Fi Aware is used or proposed for:
* nearby multiplayer gaming
* peer-to-peer file sharing
* device provisioning and IoT onboarding
* public-venue discovery services
* location-based interactions and proximity marketing
Research has explored using Wi-Fi Aware for:
* indoor localization
* crowd-awareness applications
* energy-efficient IoT communication.
Security
Wi-Fi Aware uses encryption for NAN data paths based on shared keys negotiated during discovery. Security considerations include potential metadata leakage during publish/subscribe operations, spoofing of service identifiers, and timing attacks on synchronization windows.
Mobile operating systems such as Android require user consent for applications initiating Wi-Fi Aware sessions, and may limit background access for privacy and power-management reasons.
Adoption
Wi-Fi Aware is supported on many Android phones from Google, Samsung, OnePlus, and other vendors using modern Wi-Fi chipsets that implement NAN functionality.
On Apple platforms, AWDL has historically provided peer-to-peer Wi-Fi connectivity, but EU DMA interoperability measures are expected to drive broader adoption of Wi-Fi Aware in future releases of iOS and macOS, with corresponding developer APIs documented by Apple.
ChromeOS and desktop operating systems such as Windows do not currently expose Wi-Fi Aware APIs directly to third-party developers, although underlying Wi-Fi chipsets may implement NAN capabilities.
